planting.note: Pot up divisions in spring as a houseplant; shift to a shaded porch spot in summer only once nights stay above 55F.

directions: This Logee's-bred rex begonia, hybridized by Byron Martin, carries tight spiraling leaves marked with deep red swirls over green, and unlike many rex types it skips much of the usual winter leaf drop, staying presentable through the cold months. Grow it in bright but curtain-filtered light and let the soil approach a slight wilt between waterings rather than keeping it constantly damp, which helps avoid rhizome rot. A clay pot helps wick away excess moisture, and a light monthly feed from spring through fall keeps the swirl pattern vivid.

planting.note: Grow year-round indoors in bright indirect light; this cultivar stays in leaf without the dormant rest many rex types take.

directions: Bred by Mike Kartuz, Satin Jazz is an upright rex begonia whose leaf color shifts with the seasons, running silvery with maroon borders and red veining in winter and spring and deepening to rich overall maroon by summer and fall. It keeps growing steadily year-round rather than resting, so continue light monthly feeding through most of the year and only ease off in the darkest winter weeks. Keep humidity above 50 percent and let the surface dry slightly between waterings to discourage the powdery mildew rex types are prone to.

planting.note: A compact rex suited to small pots on a bright windowsill; divide rhizomes at spring repotting.

directions: Byron Martin's Watermelon Party packs a lot of pattern into a small plant: sharply pointed, dark-edged leaves open with a pink-red watermelon-flesh center fading outward through silver to deep green veins, flecked with scattered white dots. Because it stays compact, it works well in a 4-6 inch pot grouped with other rex begonias on a humidity tray. Water only once the mix has dried enough that the plant just begins to wilt, and expect a two- to three-month winter rest when growth and color both slow down.

planting.note: Compact habit makes it a good choice for small terrariums or crowded plant-shelf displays.

directions: From the Harmony Begonias breeding line, this compact rex gets its name from a target-like leaf pattern: a dark green outer border, a pale slate-colored ring, and a crimson-red bullseye at the leaf center. Its small stature makes it an easy fit for terrariums or closed cabinets where humidity stays high, though it does fine on an open shelf if misted or grouped with other moisture-loving plants. Let the top of the mix dry before rewatering, and keep it out of direct midday sun, which can scorch the thin rex leaf surface.

planting.note: An easy-grow rex suited to beginners; blooms lightly in spring and winter.

directions: Another Byron Martin introduction from Logee's, Twisty Swirly earns its name from heart-shaped leaves up to 8 inches across that twist into a loose spiral near the base, patterned in sage green and maroon swirls. It's noted among rex begonias as an unusually forgiving grower, tolerating a bit more inconsistency in watering and light than most of its finicky cousins. Still, it flowers best and holds color longest with bright indirect light and humidity kept above 50 percent, and it will flower lightly in both spring and winter.

planting.note: Ruffled leaf margins show best with steady humidity; avoid drafts that crisp the edges.

directions: Byron Martin's Joy's Jubilee carries ruffled-edged leaves with a deep green, white-dotted outer band collapsing inward to a rich magenta center, a two-tone effect that reads almost like confetti up close. Keep humidity high and water only when the mix is nearly dry, since the thin, decorative leaf margins brown quickly if either the air or the roots stay too dry for long. Feed lightly once a month during active growth and let it rest through winter, when some leaf drop is a normal part of the cycle rather than a sign of trouble.

planting.note: Grown as much for its flower show as its foliage; let blooms rise above the leaves rather than grooming them off.

directions: Steve's Leaves Yellow Jacket is a low, oval-leaved rex with green and red foliage overlaid with silver and red markings, bred by Darren Heppel at Steve's Leaves in Texas and introduced in 2019. Per the breeder's own account it won Best New Introduction at the 2019 Southwest Region Begonia Society show and is billed as the first yellow-flowered rex begonia created; large clusters of yellow flowers with red-backed petals rise well above the leaf canopy in spring and again in fall, so give it a spot where the bloom stalks have room to stand up rather than being pinched back. Expect leaf color to mute somewhat in summer heat and intensify again as temperatures drop; let the soil dry noticeably between waterings to avoid rot.

scientific_name: Begonia rex-cultorum 'Steve's Leaves Mother of Pearl'

planting.note: Needs sustained high humidity; crisping leaf edges are a sign conditions are too dry, not a disease.

directions: Hybridized by Don Miller, Mother of Pearl is a rex begonia with a metallic pink shimmer across its leaf surface that breaks into small pearl-like flecks as it nears the margin, and no two leaves show quite the same balance of solid shimmer versus speckling. It demands humidity above 65 percent to look its best, so a closed cabinet, large terrarium, or humidity tray is worth the investment for this one over an open windowsill. Let the mix dry fairly well between waterings, since rex rhizomes are far more tolerant of underwatering than of standing moisture.

planting.note: A larger-growing rex; give it more pot room than compact cultivars to support its taller habit.

directions: Bred by Darren Heppel and introduced through Steve's Leaves, Phantom is a taller rex begonia with glossy red leaves traced in matte black veins and edges that seem to melt into the red rather than standing out sharply. Cooler weather deepens the contrast between the gloss and the matte markings, while summer heat tends to flatten and mute the color, so expect this one to look its best in fall and spring. Give it slightly more room to grow than compact rex cultivars, since it reaches 12 to 18 inches, and let it dry somewhat between waterings in bright, filtered light.

planting.note: Grows tall on canes; stake or pinch young plants to encourage branching before it reaches full height.

directions: Hybridized by Darren Heppel in 2020 and named for begonia breeder Don Miller, this cane-type angel wing begonia carries deep green wing-shaped leaves dusted with faintly shimmery white spots on sturdy jointed canes that can reach 3 to 4 feet tall. Its dangling flower clusters are white in lower light but blush pink when the plant gets more sun, making light exposure a simple way to steer the bloom color. Let the soil dry slightly between waterings, pinch young canes to build a bushier shape, and take stem cuttings in spring to start new plants easily.
